newsitem.title: MALAYSIA: FOCUS-Malaysia reforms rubber taxes,revamps sector.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Malaysia reforms rubber taxes,revamps sector.

text.p: Malaysia will make rubber processors pay a replanting and research tax in 1998 and cut the number of civil servants in the industry by nearly half, a government minister said on Monday.

The new cess (tax) system will help recover nearly 40 million ringgit ($15.8 million) a year in unpaid taxes, while three government rubber bodies would be merged into one, Primary Industries Minister Lim Keng Yaik said.

A rubber trader said the decision to collect the rubber cess from factories rather than from farmers --- which has been the case so far -- could help raise more money for replanting and research of rubber.
"But it remains to be seen if the merger is going to make the three government bodies more effective in administering the industry," he said.

Minister Lim told reporters the move would reduce by 47.74 percent the combined workforce of the Malaysian Rubber Exchange and Licensing Board, the Rubber Research Institute of Malaysia, and the Malaysian Rubber Research Development Board. A total of 1,246 civil servants will be laid off.
"The move is to have a single, more efficient Malaysian Rubber Board," he said. Both moves will take effect on January 1, 1998.

On the cess collection system, he said local rubber processing factories were allowed a discount of 13.77 cents for each kilogram (2.2 pounds) of latex they bought from farmers, as the money was supposed to be repaid to a replanting and research fund for rubber.
But due to a loophole in the law, factories only paid cess on processed rubber which they exported, and not for material they sold locally to end-consumers such as tyre manufacturers, Lim said.

"Under the current system, the cess is deducted ex-farm and farmers already pay their portion by selling cheaper to factories. But the factories are only paying the government for what they export as the collection is at the export point," said Lim.
"From January 1, 1998, we will collect the cess ex-factory, instead of ex-farm," Lim told a news conference.
He said the changes were needed as nearly 300,000 tonnes -- or about one-third of the one million tonnes of processed rubber produced by Malaysia -- was now consumed locally.
"At 13.77 cents a kg, this means that nearly 40 million ringgit is escaping our hands now," Lim said. "We want to plug this."

The cess issue caused Lim much controversy recently when the government demanded an explanation for some 600 million ringgit purportedly missing from the replanting fund of the Rubber Industry Smallholders Development Authority. Lim had to explain the money had not been missappropriated.
Lim said that about 240 million ringgit was required annually to replant some 40,000 hectares of rubber.
"But we're only collecting about 80 million ringgit now." Other measures would be instituted later to raise the required amount for replanting, Lim said.
Malaysia's rubber hectarage has dwindled from over 2.1 million hectares in the 1980s to about 1.6 million hectares now.
Officials forecast the planted area under rubber to shrink further to just about a million hectares by 2010 due to competition from other crops and space sought by property developers.
